title: LangGraph: Stateful Graphs and Durable Execution

questions.question: What does LangGraph treat as the core unit of the agent?
options: A single shared tool registry that every node reads from
A vector index over the agent's past conversation turns
A free-form LLM call with no persisted structure or state carried between turns
A state machine with typed state, function nodes, and conditional edges
questions.explanation: LangGraph models the agent as a state graph: nodes are pure functions, edges are transitions, state is typed and immutable.

questions.question: Which problem does durable execution solve?
options: Resuming a 40-step run from step 38 when it fails, with exact state, instead of starting over
Reducing the per-token inference cost of every LLM call across the entire graph, regardless of node count
Generating embeddings faster by batching them across every node in the graph
Automatically translating tool calls between different model providers mid-run
questions.explanation: Checkpoints after every node let the runtime resume from the last successful step.

questions.question: Which of these is NOT one of the three topologies LangGraph supports?
options: Supervisor, a central router LLM that dispatches to specialist subagents
Gradient ring, where nodes pass partial gradients around a closed loop
Hierarchical, supervisors managing sub-supervisors as nested subgraphs
Swarm (peer-to-peer), where agents hand off directly via a shared tool surface
questions.explanation: Topologies are supervisor, swarm, and hierarchical. Gradient ring is not a LangGraph topology.

questions.question: Why must nodes be deterministic for resume to work cleanly?
options: Model providers contractually require deterministic nodes as a condition of API access
Python's GIL requires every node function to be completely side-effect free
Resume assumes the same inputs produce the same state update; random seeds, wall-clock, and external APIs must be captured
Deterministic nodes reduce token cost because identical responses can be cached and reused across every subsequent run of the graph
questions.explanation: If a node depends on uncaptured nondeterminism, resume cannot reconstruct the post-step state.

questions.question: What is a conditional edge?
options: An edge that only fires when the runtime is executing on a GPU
An edge with a time-to-live that expires after a fixed duration
An edge weighted by the training loss recorded during a fine-tuning run
An edge chosen by a function of state, used to branch the graph
questions.explanation: Conditional edges branch based on state; overusing them makes the graph hard to reason about.

questions.question: What goes wrong when checkpoints are too small?
options: Tool state and memory writes are not recoverable; full state must serialize
The disk backing the checkpointer silently fills up and writes start failing
The graph becomes structurally unable to ever reach the END node
The model starts producing noticeably shorter answers on every turn
questions.explanation: Only checkpointing conversation turns leaves tool state and memory writes outside resume's reach.
